Open-Source Researcher Rich Tedd Says UAE Sought to Pay Him for Content Reframing Sudan War Narrative, Then Says He Received Threats After Exposing the Approach

Independent open-source researcher Rich Tedd, who tracks conflicts in Sudan and the Horn of Africa through flight monitoring and satellite imagery analysis, has published messages he says document an attempt by a UAE-linked individual to recruit him to produce paid content about Sudan. Tedd later said he began receiving direct threats after making details of the approach public.

Tedd, who posts on X under the account AfriMEOSINT, shared three screenshots from the correspondence and wrote: “The UAE’s failed attempt to put me on their payroll.”

A paid offer to reshape the narrative around Sudan’s war

According to the messages Tedd published, the person who contacted him argued that much of the current media coverage focuses on the negative conduct of the Rapid Support Militia and portrays it as the “bad guys,” while presenting the Sudanese Armed Forces as the “good guys.”

The message said the aim was to find “independent and influential journalists” who could produce material that would bring what it described as greater balance to the coverage by highlighting negative aspects of the Sudanese military’s conduct and political position.

Among the suggested themes were the Sudanese army’s relationship with Iran, alleged links to Islamist extremism, claims that battlefield developments were not moving entirely in its favor, and the argument that the army was imposing unrealistic conditions that prevented serious peace talks from beginning.

The correspondence went beyond suggesting possible story angles. It included a direct offer to pay Tedd for the content he produced, while allowing him to publish it on his own platform, provided the funder could review the material before publication to ensure that it was consistent with the objectives being pursued.

The message said:

“If so, I have a budget from which I can pay you for the content you produce. You will be able to publish it on your own platform, and all I would want is to see that particular content before publication, to make sure it aligns with what we are trying to achieve.”

That arrangement raises questions extending beyond an attempt to persuade a journalist or researcher of a particular political view. According to the text Tedd published, it combined direct funding, predetermined editorial themes and pre-publication review, while the finished material would still appear to the public as content produced independently on the researcher’s own platform.

The narrative being sought: pushing coverage toward equating the two sides

The details of what Tedd was asked to produce are particularly revealing because the message explicitly set out the narrative it wanted the content to advance.

The request was not limited to producing more critical coverage of the Sudanese army. It said the objective was to move away from a picture in which one side in the war is viewed as the “good” side and the other as the “bad” side, and toward a narrative that places the two belligerents within a more comparable moral and political frame.

That makes the correspondence more significant than a straightforward financial offer to an independent researcher. According to the text Tedd published, there was a defined editorial outcome to be pursued, followed by a list of themes that could be used to support it, including Iran, Islamists, peace negotiations and the direction of the battlefield.

This is relevant when assessing wider commentary on Sudan, particularly recurring efforts to frame the conflict as one between two essentially equivalent armed actors carrying comparable responsibility for the war and its abuses. In this instance, the correspondence published by Tedd shows that promoting such a framing was an explicit objective for which a party was prepared to fund content.

That does not mean every journalist, analyst or researcher who independently reaches a similar conclusion is acting under direction or receiving funding. Allegations of abuses by any party should be investigated and assessed on their own evidence. But the disclosure does make it important to scrutinize how particular narratives take shape, what evidence they rely on, and whether they emerge from independent analysis or are being deliberately promoted through organized and funded influence efforts.

After publishing the messages, Tedd says he received a threat

After disclosing the correspondence, Tedd published another screenshot and wrote: “And now I’m getting direct threats.”

The image shows a message from an account identified as “H,” which appeared in the screenshot to have no followers. The message included a link to a post by the open-source researcher known as Gerjon and the words: “You will be exposed soon.”

Tedd later explained why he considered the reference to Gerjon significant.

“For those who don’t know Gerjon, whose profile the Emirati guy sent me, he was one of the best OSINT and flight-tracking researchers and exposed the UAE’s covert role in fuelling wars in Sudan, Ethiopia and Libya. He later received death threats that forced him to stop his work,” Tedd wrote.

Sudanese Echo has not independently verified the identity of the individual who made the financial offer or the person behind the account that sent the subsequent message. The account of the episode is based on the correspondence and screenshots published by Tedd himself.

Kristof and Konyndyk criticize what they describe as an attempt to “buy” coverage

Tedd’s disclosures circulated widely on X and drew reactions from prominent journalists, humanitarian figures and researchers who follow Sudan.

Nicholas Kristof, the twice-Pulitzer Prize-winning New York Times columnist, responded:

“If the UAE wants better press coverage, instead of trying to buy journalists, it should stop arming brutal forces in Sudan.”

Jeremy Konyndyk, president of Refugees International and a former director of the US Office of Foreign Disaster Assistance at USAID, was similarly critical.

“This is insane! It is so revealing to see the UAE so brazenly trying to buy sympathetic media coverage for its financing of genocide in Sudan,” Konyndyk wrote.

The reactions come at a time of sustained scrutiny over the UAE’s role in Sudan’s war and its relationship with the Rapid Support Militia, amid international reporting and investigations examining supply, financing, recruitment and logistics networks benefiting the militia. Abu Dhabi has repeatedly denied supplying weapons to either side and denies involvement in the war.

Researchers studying digital influence operations have also documented networks of coordinated and inauthentic accounts promoting narratives favorable to Emirati interests or presenting the Rapid Support Militia in a more positive light. Other investigations have tracked organized online campaigns aimed at amplifying particular narratives about Sudan and flooding the information space with coordinated messaging.

Against that wider backdrop, Tedd’s account has drawn particular attention because it offers what he says is a direct example of an attempt to fund editorially guided content while preserving the outward appearance of independent research.

One commentator wrote that the UAE was “attempting to buy the world” and that “their price is complicity,” pointing to the reach of Emirati financial, political, media and digital influence. The same commentary cited the work of disinformation researcher Marc Owen Jones, who has repeatedly documented bot networks and coordinated influence operations promoting pro-UAE narratives, and researcher Thomas van Linge, who has described the Rapid Support Militia as one of the most heavily funded insurgent forces of the modern era.

What gives Tedd’s account particular weight, however, is that it does not arise from outside analysis of a bot network, a flight path or a propaganda campaign. Tedd says the offer came directly to him, with payment attached to content that would be published under his own name and on his own platform.

That is also the most consequential element of the correspondence he released. According to the messages, the proposal was not for Tedd to openly work as a spokesman or publish material carrying the name of a declared sponsor. He would remain, from the audience’s perspective, an independent researcher, while another party funded the content, suggested the themes to emphasize and reviewed the material before publication.

After Tedd rejected the offer and published the messages, the episode quickly expanded from an undisclosed financial approach into a wider debate over paid influence, covert messaging and the pressures faced by independent researchers covering Sudan.

In an information environment already shaped by propaganda, influence campaigns and competing narratives surrounding Sudan’s war, Tedd’s disclosure leaves a broader question hanging over the debate: if one researcher received such an offer, rejected it and exposed it publicly, how many similar approaches may never have come to light?

A research paper is being presented as evidence that universities teach courses about Meghan’s Mole aka Niloofar Purrahnama. The evidence does not support that claim.

An October 6 post from @entylawyer, who is also a liar,  alleged that an unnamed royal YouTuber was being mentioned in European university classes and that entire SEO courses were using her social media as an example of truth overcoming bots and celebrity PR. Meghan’s Mole shared the post approvingly.

According to the viewer who supplied screenshots, Meghan’s Mole subsequently showed an academic article on her programme and said she received it from The Royal Grift. The screenshots identify the publication, allowing its contents to be checked directly.

The paper is genuine. The university-course claim remains unsubstantiated.

The article was written by Mª Milagros del Saz-Rubio of the Universitat Politècnica de València in Spain and published in Poznan Studies in Contemporary Linguistics in 2024. Its subject is negative language about Meghan Markle, rather than a course about Meghan’s Mole. (https://t.co/Mx4iatPeQ0)

The study analysed 5,698 tweets and manually examined a random sample of 400. Niloofar was NOT the the only tweet analyzed. Its focus was hostility, evaluative language, and gender stereotypes. Crucially, the researcher explained:

> “I anonymized the tweets by deleting the posters’ IDs and obscuring the identity of the person they were replying to.”

She also explicitly stated that she did not endorse the views expressed in the tweets. The published examples therefore cannot establish that Meghan’s Mole authored them. (https://t.co/EDNCSe7qUL)

The conclusion discusses how hostile tweets can perpetuate sexism, misogyny, and traditional stereotypes about women. It does not certify the commenters as truth-tellers. The insults appearing in the article’s title are language under examination—not findings that those descriptions of Meghan Markle are accurate. (https://t.co/EDNCSe7qUL)

Searches of the accessible full text found no mention of “Mole,” “Grift,” or “SEO.” (https://t.co/EDNCSe7qUL, https://t.co/EDNCSe7qUL, https://t.co/EDNCSe7qUL)

The distinction matters:

A university researcher publishing an article, a lecturer mentioning an account, and an institution offering an entire course are three different things. Evidence for one cannot simply be substituted for another.

The wider search also uncovered questionable articles on education-related domains.

Pages on https://t.co/GQPCH1yUOm and https://t.co/CaWAWDS551 carried an article with the same title, opening text, author label “bejo,” and number “6909.” Neither supplied a named lecturer, course title, or syllabus demonstrating that Meghan’s Mole’s work was being taught. Duplicated text on different websites is not independent corroboration. (https://t.co/GQPCH1yUOm, https://t.co/CaWAWDS551)

The MENA page also displayed supposed PDF download buttons pointing to an unrelated domain, https://t.co/f3FTC7QbAr, accompanied by a claim that no viruses had been detected. Those buttons were not evidence of a university course. (https://t.co/CaWAWDS551)

Another article on https://t.co/EQZENMijyM, labelled “Alliance University,” used the same “bejo” author label and “6909” number. It included an unrelated birthday-cake image and a link about Lowe’s jobs, while providing no documentation of the alleged teaching. (https://t.co/EQZENMijyM)

These features are consistent with mass-produced SEO content or spam. That is an assessment of the pages, not proof of who created them or how they appeared on those domains. 

The newly identified academic article should be distinguished from those questionable webpages. It is a legitimate publication; the problem is the unsupported claim being attached to it.

Receiving an article from another YouTuber does not establish that universities teach courses about an account. Sharing a blind item does not independently verify it. And anonymised research examples cannot be claimed as recognition of a particular creator without additional evidence.

The claim remains unsubstantiated. The article shown does not prove it.

To substantiate it, provide the university’s name, the instructor’s name, the course title, and a syllabus or direct institutional confirmation. Until then, there is a documented research paper about online language directed at Meghan Markle—and an unsupported claim about courses celebrating Meghan’s Mole.

第1003期 小路和你读AI论文。今日4篇高质量论文。

1. 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗦𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴: 𝗦𝗙𝗧 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝘀 𝗕𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗧𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸（《带采样的微调：SFT 比你想的更会学》）

链接：https://t.co/QXVXbqz5hu

作者背景：Aayush Karan, Sitan Chen, Yilun Du, Harvard

不改损失，用 MCMC 把离策略专家轨迹逐步改写成更接近参考模型的在策略分布，SFT 在泛化与遗忘上就能比肩强在策略后训练。实验覆盖科学技能、数学推理和开放式专长。采样本身可以当作后训练原语，这会动摇"保能力必须上 RL"的默认做法，做后训练的人值得细看。

2. 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗥𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗙𝗶𝘁: 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹-𝗛𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗰𝗿𝗼𝘀𝘀 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗧𝗮𝘀𝗸𝘀（《找到合适的搭配：跨 Agent 任务的模型与 Harness 交互》）

链接：https://t.co/txmUWsp8E5

作者背景：Yixuan Li, Bo An 等

模型、harness 与任务必须放在一起评，强模型和厂商自有脚手架都不会稳定领先。66 组配置横跨 OpenHands、DeepSeek Harness、PI、openJiuwen 与三项命令行 agent 基准。Terminal-Bench 4 上，Claude 在 OpenHands 中领先 GPT 7.94 分，在 PI 中落后 30.16 分，五个模型里有四个的最优 harness 随基准改变。作者发布了适配器、评测代码和 6,204 条轨迹，部署 agent 的人可以直接拿来做选型证据。

3. 𝗛𝗶𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝘂𝗼𝘂𝘀 𝗗𝗶𝗳𝗳𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗟𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀（《分层连续扩散语言模型》）

链接：https://t.co/dC0fv3j4PU

作者背景：Alexander Schwing（UIUC）等

让连续潜变量成为唯一持续生成状态，token 每步读出并回馈，以缓解离散扩散并行解码时的独立采样断裂。训练目标来自 token 似然的变分界，同规模下在 Sudoku、Countdown 和 LM1B 上优于离散与连续扩散基线。做扩散语言模型的人可以看看它是否真正保住了并行解码中的 token 依赖。

4. 𝗘𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗔𝗯𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗜𝘀 𝗮 𝗗𝗼𝘀𝗲: 𝗖𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘄𝗲𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗦𝗲𝗹𝗳-𝗥𝗲𝗽𝗮𝗶𝗿（《每次消融都是一剂药：反权重与"自修复"的假象》）

链接：https://t.co/IzLv2zqidD

消融后看似补偿的响应，多半来自干预前就存在的反权重，它们随对比强度作仿射响应，与临时自我修复无关。在事实判决任务上，Gemma、Qwen、LLaMA、Mistral 的 81 个下游方向中有 68 个服从该仿射律。GPT-2 Small 的 IOI 电路里，干预能触及的 10 个头有 7 个符合，且全是反权重，斜率还能由固定权重预先估计。做机制可解释性的人可以拿它校准对自修复的判断。

How to design rewards for post-training frontier image models? 

Our research suggests human preference reward is necessary, but insufficient: A preference model may still reward outputs that look appealing but miss details, introduce unrequested content, or exhibit other forms of reward-hacking.

We therefore optimize towards a composite reward:
- Bradley-Terry reward model trained on ~5.6M pairwise human votes
- Faithfulness reward from auto-generated prompt checklists evaluated by a vision-language model
- Constraint reward covering explicit and implicit user intent
- Anti-reward-hacking rubric rewards targeting failures such as garbled text and photorealism drift
This post-training recipe improves two already-strong open image models:
- Post-trained FLUX.2-dev gains 69 Elo points on our live T2I leaderboard, scoring 1202
- Post-trained Ideogram 4 gains 20 Elo points reaching a score of 1224 and surpassing all publicly listed open models (as of Sep 04, 2026).

Offline ablations with Gemini 3.5 Flash as the judge, show that these reward components are complementary: win rate against the base model increases as we add faithfulness and then constraint rewards on top of preference-only training, reaching 64.2%.

Finally, we ensemble policies trained with and without the anti-reward-hacking objective directly in weight space, further increasing win rate to 66.0%.
